title: COPD: Confirm Obstruction, Prevent Exacerbations
bottomLine: COPD requires compatible symptoms/exposures plus persistent airflow obstruction on spirometry. Treatment should reduce symptoms and exacerbations, with smoking cessation, vaccination and inhaled long-acting bronchodilation forming the core of care.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, chronic cough/sputum and tobacco or occupational exposure are common.
Exacerbation means sustained worsening beyond usual day-to-day variation.
differentiate: Asthma has variable airflow obstruction and often earlier onset; heart failure, anemia, deconditioning and ILD can mimic COPD.
assessment: Assess smoking/exposure history, symptom burden, prior exacerbations/hospitalizations, inhaler technique, oxygenation and comorbidity.
workup: Confirm stable COPD with post-bronchodilator spirometry; chest imaging is used when another diagnosis or complication is suspected.
management: Use CTS-guided long-acting bronchodilator therapy matched to symptoms/exacerbation history; add inhaled corticosteroid selectively rather than automatically.
Acute exacerbations require bronchodilator intensification and selective systemic corticosteroid/antibiotic use based on severity and features.
medicationSafety: Long-term inhaled corticosteroid can increase pneumonia risk in some patients; check indication.
Oxygen is titrated to clinical need; chronic home oxygen requires formal criteria.
counselling: Smoking cessation is the most important disease-modifying intervention; teach inhaler technique and action plan.
followUp: Reassess symptoms, exacerbations, inhaler use and pulmonary rehabilitation eligibility.
examTrap: Diagnosing COPD from smoking history and chronic cough without spirometry when the patient is stable enough for confirmation.
oneLinePearl: COPD is spirometry-confirmed persistent obstruction, not a smoking label.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2023 COPD pharmacotherapy guideline

title: Pneumothorax: Stable Air Leak or Tension Physiology?
bottomLine: Sudden unilateral pleuritic pain and dyspnea with reduced breath sounds suggests pneumothorax. Hemodynamic compromise or severe respiratory distress makes tension pneumothorax a clinical emergency requiring immediate decompression before imaging.
recognize: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax often occurs without known lung disease; secondary pneumothorax is less tolerated because reserve is reduced.
differentiate: PE, ACS, pneumonia and musculoskeletal pain can mimic it.
Tension physiology is defined by obstructive shock, not by radiographic size alone.
assessment: Assess ABCs, oxygenation, respiratory distress, unilateral breath sounds, tracheal shift when late, JVP and shock.
workup: Use chest radiography or bedside ultrasound in stable patients; do not delay emergency decompression for imaging when tension is clinically apparent.
management: Management depends on stability, size, symptoms and underlying lung disease; tension pneumothorax needs immediate decompression followed by definitive chest drainage.
medicationSafety: Positive-pressure ventilation can worsen an untreated pneumothorax.
counselling: Discuss recurrence risk, smoking cessation and restrictions on air travel/diving according to specialist guidance.
followUp: Ensure radiographic resolution and specialist review when recurrent or secondary.
examTrap: Sending an unstable patient for chest x-ray before treating suspected tension pneumothorax.
oneLinePearl: Tension pneumothorax is treated clinically, not after radiology confirms it.
sourceBasis: Canadian emergency and thoracic practice principles

title: Pleural Effusion: Transudate, Exudate, or Infection?
bottomLine: A new unilateral or unexplained pleural effusion usually needs cause-directed evaluation. Heart failure can cause transudative effusions, while infection, malignancy and inflammatory disease commonly produce exudates.
recognize: Dyspnea, pleuritic pain, reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion are typical.
differentiate: Bilateral effusions in clear decompensated heart failure may respond to diuresis without immediate diagnostic tap; unilateral, febrile or atypical effusions deserve more evaluation.
assessment: Assess heart failure, infection, malignancy, PE, liver/renal disease and medication history.
workup: Use chest imaging and diagnostic thoracentesis when the cause is uncertain or complicated infection/malignancy is possible; classify fluid using accepted biochemical criteria.
management: Treat the cause; complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema requires drainage plus antimicrobials.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulation and procedural bleeding risk before thoracentesis according to local policy.
counselling: Explain why fluid analysis may be needed even when symptoms improve temporarily after drainage.
followUp: Track resolution and ensure malignancy/infection results are closed-loop.
examTrap: Assuming every pleural effusion in a patient with heart failure is cardiac despite unilateral fever and pleuritic pain.
oneLinePearl: Unexplained unilateral pleural fluid deserves a diagnosis, not just a diuretic.

title: Hemoptysis: Airway Risk Before Etiology
bottomLine: Hemoptysis ranges from blood-streaked sputum to life-threatening airway flooding. First determine severity and airway/hemodynamic stability, then evaluate infection, malignancy, bronchiectasis, PE, anticoagulation and other causes.
recognize: True hemoptysis arises from the lower respiratory tract; hematemesis and nasopharyngeal bleeding can mimic it.
differentiate: Massive/life-threatening hemoptysis is defined functionally by respiratory or hemodynamic threat rather than a precise volume cutoff.
assessment: Assess airway, oxygenation, bleeding rate, anticoagulants, smoking, TB risk, infection symptoms, VTE risk and cancer features.
workup: Chest imaging is required for concerning or recurrent hemoptysis; CT and bronchoscopy are selected according to stability and suspected source.
management: Life-threatening bleeding needs emergency airway/interventional management; reverse anticoagulation when clinically indicated and treat the cause.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants and antiplatelets may worsen bleeding but should not be stopped reflexively without considering indication and severity in stable minor cases.
counselling: Recurrent hemoptysis requires reassessment even if prior episodes were labelled bronchitis.
followUp: Ensure imaging and specialist results are reviewed until the cause is resolved.
examTrap: Estimating blood volume instead of recognizing that the airway is becoming compromised.
oneLinePearl: In hemoptysis, the immediate danger is often airway obstruction, not exsanguination.
sourceBasis: Canadian respiratory and emergency practice principles

title: Pulmonary Nodule and Lung Cancer: Risk-Stratify the Finding
bottomLine: An incidental pulmonary nodule is not automatically cancer and must not be ignored. Follow-up depends on size, morphology, growth and patient cancer risk; symptoms or suspicious imaging accelerate evaluation.
recognize: Smoking, age, prior cancer, upper-lobe location, spiculation and growth raise malignancy risk.
Weight loss, persistent hemoptysis, unexplained hoarseness or recurrent focal pneumonia are concerning.
differentiate: Granuloma and benign nodules are common; screening pathways differ from diagnostic evaluation of symptomatic patients.
assessment: Document smoking pack-years, occupational exposures, prior imaging, cancer history and symptoms.
workup: Compare with prior imaging and use a validated nodule follow-up pathway; PET/biopsy is reserved for higher-risk lesions.
management: Refer suspected malignancy promptly to a lung diagnostic pathway; offer smoking cessation regardless of diagnosis.
medicationSafety: Do not delay evaluation by repeatedly prescribing antibiotics for persistent focal symptoms without reassessment.
counselling: Explain that surveillance is active management and give the exact next imaging date.
followUp: Create a closed-loop tracking system for every nodule requiring surveillance.
examTrap: Using a population screening interval for a symptomatic patient with a suspicious lesion.
oneLinePearl: A nodule needs a risk-based plan and an owner for follow-up.
sourceBasis: Canadian lung cancer screening and diagnostic pathway principles

title: Tuberculosis: Identify Infectious Pulmonary Disease Early
bottomLine: Chronic cough, fever/night sweats, weight loss or abnormal chest imaging plus epidemiologic risk should trigger pulmonary TB assessment and infection-control precautions. Latent TB infection and active TB disease are fundamentally different.
recognize: Risk rises with close exposure, birth/residence in high-incidence regions, homelessness/crowding, immunosuppression and certain Indigenous communities affected by structural inequities.
differentiate: TST/IGRA support TB infection but do not rule active disease in or out alone; active pulmonary TB requires microbiologic/imaging assessment.
assessment: Assess symptoms, exposure, travel/residence, immune status, prior TB treatment and pregnancy.
workup: For suspected active pulmonary TB, obtain chest imaging and appropriate respiratory specimens for molecular testing/culture under public-health guidance.
management: Use airborne precautions and involve public health/infectious disease; active TB requires multidrug treatment and adherence support.
medicationSafety: TB drugs have important hepatic, ocular and drug-interaction risks requiring structured monitoring.
counselling: Use culturally safe, non-stigmatizing communication and address housing, transportation and medication-access barriers.
followUp: Coordinate public-health contact management and treatment completion.
examTrap: Calling a positive IGRA active tuberculosis without evaluating for disease.
oneLinePearl: IGRA/TST detects infection; symptoms, imaging and microbiology determine active disease.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada Canadian Tuberculosis Standards

title: Interstitial Lung Disease: Restriction Is Not Asthma
bottomLine: Progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, inspiratory crackles and restrictive physiology should raise ILD rather than repeated asthma/COPD treatment. Early recognition matters because causes and treatments differ.
recognize: Fine bibasilar crackles, clubbing, hypoxemia and restrictive pulmonary-function patterns are clues.
differentiate: Obstructive spirometry supports asthma/COPD; heart failure can mimic ILD but has different imaging/hemodynamic features.
assessment: Ask connective-tissue symptoms, bird/mould exposures, occupational dusts, radiation and medications associated with lung toxicity.
workup: Use full PFTs and high-resolution CT; serology and exposure testing are directed by phenotype.
management: Refer suspected fibrotic ILD to respirology; remove offending exposures/drugs and treat specific inflammatory/fibrotic disease where indicated.
medicationSafety: Before immunosuppression, screen for infections and vaccination needs according to current CTS guidance.
counselling: Discuss pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination, smoking cessation and oxygen when indicated.
followUp: Trend symptoms, PFTs, oxygenation and imaging through specialty care.
examTrap: Escalating inhaled bronchodilators for progressive restrictive disease with inspiratory crackles.
oneLinePearl: Dry cough plus crackles plus restriction should make you think interstitium.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society ILD standards and 2026 immunosuppression infection-screening statement

title: Work-Related Asthma: Ask Whether Symptoms Improve Away From Work
bottomLine: Asthma symptoms that worsen during work periods and improve on weekends or vacation should trigger occupational assessment before exposure continues and disease becomes harder to reverse.
recognize: High-risk exposures include sensitizing chemicals, flour, isocyanates, laboratory animals and irritant events.
differentiate: Work-exacerbated pre-existing asthma differs from new sensitizer-induced occupational asthma, but both require exposure control.
assessment: Take a detailed job/task/exposure history and symptom timing relative to shifts and time away.
workup: Confirm asthma objectively and use serial peak flows or specialty testing across work/off-work periods when appropriate.
management: Control asthma and reduce/remove harmful exposure; early occupational medicine/respirology referral can preserve function.
medicationSafety: Escalating medication without addressing the exposure is incomplete treatment.
counselling: Discuss workplace accommodation and compensation/reporting pathways according to jurisdiction.
followUp: Document objective findings and exposure timeline carefully.
examTrap: Treating recurrent Monday-to-Friday asthma flares without asking what the patient does at work.
oneLinePearl: The work history is a diagnostic test in occupational asthma.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society occupational asthma principles

title: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency: COPD That Does Not Fit
bottomLine: Consider alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency when COPD/emphysema occurs young, with little smoking exposure, basilar emphysema, unexplained liver disease or family history. CTS issued updated targeted-testing guidance in 2025.
recognize: Early emphysema, bronchiectasis and liver disease can occur.
differentiate: Smoking-related COPD remains common, but inherited deficiency changes counselling and family implications.
assessment: Ask age at onset, smoking, occupational exposure, liver disease and first-degree family history.
workup: Use serum AAT level with confirmatory phenotype/genotype testing when indicated.
management: Smoking avoidance/cessation and standard COPD care are essential; selected severe deficiency may qualify for specialist-directed augmentation therapy.
medicationSafety: Augmentation therapy is specialized and should not be offered solely from a low screening level without confirmation and eligibility assessment.
counselling: Offer genetic counselling/family testing discussion without coercion.
followUp: Coordinate respirology and hepatology follow-up as phenotype requires.
examTrap: Assuming all COPD in a smoker is fully explained by smoking despite unusually early severe disease.
oneLinePearl: Young or disproportionate emphysema deserves an alpha-1 question.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2025 Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency guideline

title: Aspiration Syndromes: Pneumonitis Is Not Automatically Pneumonia
bottomLine: A witnessed aspiration can cause chemical pneumonitis without bacterial infection. Antibiotics are reserved for a clinical bacterial aspiration pneumonia pattern rather than given reflexively after every aspiration event.
recognize: Risk rises with dysphagia, stroke, dementia, sedation, vomiting, impaired consciousness and tube feeding.
differentiate: Abrupt hypoxemia soon after aspiration may be chemical pneumonitis; later fever, purulent sputum and persistent infiltrate can support bacterial pneumonia.
assessment: Assess airway/oxygenation, swallowing history, consciousness, dentition, reflux/vomiting and recurrent chest infections.
workup: Chest imaging and cultures are selected by severity; swallowing assessment is important when aspiration risk persists.
management: Support oxygenation and airway clearance; treat confirmed bacterial pneumonia and address swallowing/positioning/oral care risk factors.
medicationSafety: Sedatives and anticholinergics can worsen swallowing or consciousness; review them.
counselling: Teach safe feeding strategies through speech-language pathology recommendations rather than generic thickening advice.
followUp: Reassess dysphagia and medication contributors after the acute episode.
examTrap: Starting broad-spectrum antibiotics solely because aspiration was witnessed before signs of bacterial infection emerge.
oneLinePearl: Aspiration event plus inflammation is not automatically aspiration pneumonia.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada antimicrobial stewardship principles

title: Influenza and COVID-19: Identify Who Needs Antiviral Treatment
bottomLine: Most uncomplicated viral respiratory infections are supportive-care illnesses, but high-risk or severely ill patients may benefit from timely antiviral therapy. Treatment eligibility changes with circulating pathogens, drug authorizations and public-health guidance.
recognize: Older age, pregnancy, immunocompromise and major chronic disease increase complication risk.
differentiate: Clinical symptoms overlap substantially; testing is useful when the result changes treatment, isolation or outbreak management.
assessment: Assess illness duration, severity, oxygenation, hydration, pregnancy, immune status, comorbidity, medication interactions and outbreak setting.
workup: Use current local/public-health testing strategy; chest imaging is not routine for uncomplicated viral illness.
management: Provide supportive care and current antiviral treatment for eligible patients using contemporary Canadian guidance; escalate pneumonia, hypoxemia or clinical deterioration.
medicationSafety: COVID antivirals can have major drug interactions and renal dosing requirements; medication reconciliation is essential.
counselling: Discuss vaccination, staying home when acutely ill and current infection-control recommendations.
followUp: High-risk patients need clear early return precautions because treatment windows are time-sensitive.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics for uncomplicated influenza or COVID-19 without evidence of bacterial coinfection.
oneLinePearl: Viral does not always mean no treatment—but it does mean antibiotics need a bacterial reason.

title: Chronic Cough: Do Not Skip the Chest X-Ray and Medication Review
bottomLine: Chronic cough is commonly related to upper-airway disease, asthma/eosinophilic airway disease, reflux or ACE-inhibitor use, but red flags and abnormal imaging require a different pathway.
recognize: Duration, triggers, sputum, wheeze, nasal symptoms, reflux, smoking and medication timing are diagnostically useful.
differentiate: ACE-inhibitor cough can begin after treatment starts and resolves after withdrawal; chronic cough with hemoptysis or weight loss is not a routine empiric-treatment problem.
assessment: Review smoking/vaping, ACE inhibitor use, occupational exposures, TB risk, reflux, rhinitis and asthma symptoms.
workup: Obtain chest radiography for persistent unexplained cough and spirometry when asthma/COPD is plausible; further tests depend on findings.
management: Treat identified causes sequentially and reassess response rather than stacking multiple empiric therapies indefinitely.
medicationSafety: Avoid long-term opioid cough suppressants without a clear indication and specialist context.
counselling: Explain that cough resolution may lag after the trigger is removed.
followUp: Revisit the differential when cough persists despite appropriate trials.
examTrap: Adding a PPI, antihistamine and inhaler simultaneously without establishing which syndrome is actually present.
oneLinePearl: Chronic cough needs a sequence, not a medication pile.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory practice resources
